South Korea’s Agriculture Industry Faces Mounting Debt Crisis, Farms Struggle to Stay Afloat

SEOUL, June 14 — South Korea’s agriculture industry is reeling from a deepening debt crisis, as a wave of loan defaults and a tightening credit market threaten the survival of many farms across the country. Industry groups and government officials warn that the ongoing crisis is putting severe pressure on agricultural firms, farming sites, and workers, with no clear resolution in sight.

The crisis intensified this spring after a sharp decline in crop prices, leaving many farmers unable to service loans taken out during earlier periods of expansion. According to the Korean Federation of Agricultural Cooperatives, the total outstanding debt in the agriculture sector surpassed 42 trillion won ($30.3 billion) in May — a year-on-year increase of 18 percent. Local banks and lending cooperatives have responded by sharply scaling back new loans and calling in outstanding credit lines, further straining producers.

“Many of our members are on the brink of insolvency,” said Kim Tae-hoon, chairman of the National Farmers’ Trade Union. “With prices so low and credit disappearing, operating costs can’t be covered. We’re seeing layoffs and even closures on family-run farms that have been in business for generations.”

In the farming regions of Jeolla and Gyeongsang provinces, growers report plummeting demand for staple crops such as rice and cabbage, while livestock producers face similar declines. The drop in prices has been attributed in part to a glut of supply and weakening export orders. Farmers say they are now struggling to pay for seeds, fertilizer, and equipment maintenance, with some forced to leave fields fallow or sell off livestock.

The Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs said it is monitoring the situation and considering emergency measures. “We recognize the seriousness of the debt burden facing agricultural firms and are reviewing support programs, including the possibility of loan restructuring and temporary credit guarantees,” said deputy minister Lee Ji-won at a press conference in Seoul.

Workers at major agricultural sites have begun to feel the impact, as layoffs and wage cuts spread throughout the sector. “We’ve had to let go of over a third of our labor force in the past month,” said Park Min-kyu, director of operations at Hanrim Agro, a large rice producer. “Many workers are worried about how to provide for their families.”

Industry analysts warn that unless credit conditions improve or new support measures are introduced soon, the crisis could worsen in the coming weeks. “The agriculture sector is under extreme financial stress,” said Lim Soo-yeon, senior analyst at the Korea Rural Economy Institute. “Immediate intervention will be necessary to prevent widespread bankruptcies.”
